author: hamilton
title: What Is at Stake
summary: Hamilton opens the series by telling New Yorkers that the old government has failed and they must decide on a new Constitution. He says America will show the world whether people can create good government through careful thought and choice, instead of by accident or force. He asks readers to judge the plan on its merits, warns that people on both sides have mixed motives, and lists the topics the series will cover.

author: jay
title: One People, One Nation
summary: Jay argues that Americans are already one people, joined by geography, language, religion, and the shared fight for independence. Splitting into separate countries would throw that away. He praises the Convention's members and reminds readers that the earlier Continental Congress also gave good advice that people were wrong to doubt.

author: jay
title: Fewer Reasons for War
summary: Jay argues that a single national government will give foreign countries fewer reasons to go to war with America. It will keep treaties more faithfully and handle disputes more calmly than thirteen separate states, especially border states tempted to act rashly.

author: jay
title: Strength Discourages Attack
summary: Jay warns that foreign nations may start wars for selfish reasons, such as competition over trade and fishing. A united America, able to organize its defense under one plan, will look strong enough to discourage attacks. A divided America would invite them.

author: jay
title: Rival Confederacies Would Be Enemies
summary: Jay predicts that if America split into several smaller confederacies, they would become jealous rivals. Each might seek foreign allies against the others, just as England and Scotland did before they united. Disunion would invite foreign powers to play Americans against each other.

author: hamilton
title: Neighbors Become Enemies
summary: Hamilton argues that independent states sitting side by side would eventually fight. People are ambitious, jealous, and greedy, and nations act on those passions. He rejects the idea that trade makes countries peaceful, pointing to history, where trading republics went to war as often as anyone.

author: hamilton
title: What the States Would Fight Over
summary: Hamilton lists the specific issues that could start wars between separated states: claims to western land, trade rules that favor one state over another, how to split the national war debt, and laws that cheat out-of-state creditors.

author: hamilton
title: War Between States Would Destroy Liberty
summary: Hamilton warns that constant danger from neighboring states would force each one to keep a standing army. Over time the military would grow more powerful than civilian government, and freedom would be lost. A united America, protected by oceans like Britain, could avoid that fate.

author: hamilton
title: A Union Protects Against Faction and Rebellion
summary: Hamilton admits that small republics in history were torn apart by conflict. But he says the new 'science of politics' has found fixes: separating powers, checks and balances, judges who serve for life, and representation. He uses the writer Montesquieu to show that a union of states can enjoy the benefits of both small and large republics.

author: madison
title: How a Large Republic Controls Factions
summary: The most famous essay. Madison defines a faction as a group whose goals go against other people's rights or the good of the whole community. Factions come from human nature, so the causes can't be removed without destroying liberty. Instead, the effects must be controlled. A large republic that uses elected representatives contains so many different interests that no single faction can easily take over.

author: hamilton
title: Union Makes America a Trading Power
summary: Hamilton argues that a united nation can bargain with Europe over trade, build a navy, and protect American shipping. Divided states would be pushed around by European powers. He urges Americans to build a strong nation of their own instead of serving European greatness.

author: hamilton
title: Union Makes Taxes Easier to Collect
summary: Hamilton explains that trade creates wealth, and taxes on imports are the easiest way for a government to raise money. A single national government can collect those taxes well, because smugglers can't simply slip goods across state borders.

author: hamilton
title: One Government Costs Less
summary: A short essay arguing that one national government would cost taxpayers less than the several separate governments that would exist if the Union broke up into regional confederacies.

author: madison
title: A Republic Can Work Across a Large Country
summary: Madison answers critics who say America is too big to be a republic. They confuse a democracy, where citizens meet and govern in person, with a republic, where they elect representatives. A republic can stretch much farther. He also notes that the national government has limited powers and the states keep the rest. He urges Americans not to fear new ideas, since the Revolution itself was something new.

author: hamilton
title: The Old Government Is Broken
summary: Hamilton describes how bad things are under the Articles of Confederation: unpaid debts, no respect abroad, and a collapsing economy. The basic flaw is that Congress can only make requests of the states, not laws for individual people. Without a way to enforce its decisions, a government is not really a government.

author: hamilton
title: Forcing States to Obey Means War
summary: Hamilton explains that a government that acts on states can only enforce its rules by using armies against them, which is civil war. A real national government must reach individual citizens directly through its own laws, officers, and courts.

author: hamilton
title: The States Will Stay Strong
summary: Hamilton answers the fear that a national government will swallow up the states. He argues that the states handle the everyday matters people care about most, like local justice, so they will keep people's loyalty. History shows that local powers usually overpower central ones, not the other way around.

author: madison-hamilton
title: Lessons from Ancient Greece
summary: A history lesson on leagues of ancient Greek city-states. Their central councils were too weak to keep members in line, which led to internal fighting and finally conquest by Macedon.

author: madison-hamilton
title: Lessons from Germany, Poland, and Switzerland
summary: More history: the loosely joined states of the Holy Roman Empire, Poland, and Switzerland. In each case, a weak central government acting on member states produced disorder, foreign meddling, and weakness.

author: madison-hamilton
title: Lessons from the Dutch Republic
summary: The Netherlands shows the same problem. Its central government depended on member provinces, so it constantly broke its own rules to function. The lesson: a government over other governments, rather than over individuals, does not work.

author: hamilton
title: More Flaws in the Articles
summary: Hamilton lists further defects of the Articles of Confederation: Congress has no way to enforce its laws, no power to protect a state government from rebellion (as in Shays' Rebellion), and an unfair system for asking states to contribute money.

author: hamilton
title: Still More Flaws in the Articles
summary: Hamilton points to more failures: no power to regulate trade, a clumsy way of raising armies, equal votes for big and small states, the need for supermajorities that let a few block the many, and no national courts. Worst of all, the Articles were never approved by the people themselves, who are the true source of a government's power.

author: hamilton
title: Defense Requires Real Power
summary: Hamilton argues that the government responsible for national defense must have enough power to do the job. Since no one can predict future dangers, the power to provide for defense should not be limited in advance. The means must match the ends.

author: hamilton
title: Answering Fears About Standing Armies
summary: Hamilton responds to fears about a permanent army in peacetime. Congress, elected by the people, controls the army, and it must approve military funding at least every two years. Most state constitutions don't ban peacetime armies either, and America's frontier needs protection.

author: hamilton
title: Defense Can't Be Left to the States
summary: Hamilton explains why defense must be a national job, not left to individual states. He argues that a strict ban on peacetime armies would simply be ignored in a crisis, and that the Revolution proved militias alone are not enough.

author: hamilton
title: Limiting Congress on Defense
summary: Hamilton argues against tying Congress's hands on defense. The real protections are that army funding expires every two years, so it must be openly debated, and that state governments and the people will watch closely for any misuse.

author: hamilton
title: People Will Obey a Good Government
summary: Hamilton predicts that a well-run national government will earn people's respect and obedience without needing force. As it becomes part of daily life, people will grow familiar with it. Its laws, made under the Constitution, become the supreme law of the land.

author: hamilton
title: When Force Is Needed and the People's Defense
summary: Hamilton admits that any government may sometimes need force to put down rebellion. But if the national government ever abused power, the states and the people would be ready to resist it. A large country also makes tyranny harder to establish.

author: hamilton
title: The Militia
summary: Hamilton defends giving Congress power to organize and train the militia (citizen soldiers), while the states appoint the officers. A well-trained militia actually reduces the need for a standing army, and the fear that it will be used against the people is exaggerated.

author: hamilton
title: Government Needs Money
summary: Hamilton calls money the lifeblood of government. Under the Articles, Congress could only ask states for money, and they often didn't pay. The national government needs its own power to tax, which will also let it borrow in emergencies.

author: hamilton
title: The Logic of the Taxing Power
summary: Hamilton starts from basic principles: a government's powers should match its responsibilities. Since national needs can't be predicted, the taxing power should be general. He argues that fear of the national government overpowering the states is speculation.

author: hamilton
title: States Keep Their Power to Tax
summary: Hamilton explains that the states keep their own power to tax, except on imports and exports. The states keep every power they had unless the Constitution clearly gives it only to the national government, forbids it to the states, or makes state use of it impossible.

author: hamilton
title: The 'Necessary and Proper' and 'Supremacy' Clauses
summary: Hamilton defends two clauses critics called dangerous. The 'necessary and proper' clause just states what is already implied: a government can pass the laws it needs to carry out its powers. The supremacy clause makes national laws supreme, but only laws made in line with the Constitution. Laws that go beyond the Constitution are not supreme.

author: hamilton
title: Planning for Future Needs
summary: Hamilton argues that the national government's revenue can't be limited to import taxes. Future wars and emergencies will be expensive and unpredictable, and the government must be able to meet them.

author: hamilton
title: Who Represents Whom?
summary: Hamilton argues that relying only on import taxes would hurt the economy. He also answers the claim that Congress must include members of every job or class. Merchants, landowners, and professionals will share interests with many citizens and can represent them well.

author: hamilton
title: Taxes and Representation, Continued
summary: Hamilton continues the argument about representation and answers fears of internal taxes. He says the national government can use state knowledge and officials to collect taxes fairly, and that people won't be crushed by double taxation.

author: madison
title: Why the Convention's Job Was So Hard
summary: Madison asks readers to judge the Constitution fairly by understanding how hard it was to write. The Convention had to combine strong government with liberty, draw a line between state and national power, and balance large and small states. Even human language is too imprecise to define everything perfectly. That the delegates agreed at all is remarkable.

author: madison
title: The Critics Contradict Each Other
summary: Madison points out that ancient governments were usually designed by a single lawgiver, not a group. He then shows how the Constitution's critics contradict one another, attacking it for opposite reasons. Meanwhile, the Articles have far worse flaws. It makes no sense to reject a better plan because it isn't perfect.

author: madison
title: Is the Plan Truly Republican?
summary: Madison defines a republic: a government that gets all its power from the people and is run by people who hold office for limited terms or during good behavior. The Constitution passes this test. He then shows that the new government is neither purely national nor purely federal but a mix of both.

author: madison
title: Did the Convention Have the Authority?
summary: Critics said the Convention was only supposed to revise the Articles, not replace them. Madison argues that the delegates were told to create a government adequate to the country's needs, which required big changes. In any case the plan is only a proposal. The people themselves will decide whether to adopt it.

author: madison
title: Powers for Security
summary: Madison begins reviewing the Constitution's powers, starting with war and defense. A nation must be able to defend itself, and limits on this power would be ignored in an emergency anyway. He also argues that the 'general welfare' phrase does not give Congress unlimited power, because the list of specific powers that follows defines it.

author: madison
title: Powers over Foreign Affairs and Trade Between States
summary: Madison explains powers over treaties, ambassadors, foreign trade, trade between the states, money, citizenship, and bankruptcy. He defends the clause that allows the slave trade to be banned after 1808 as an improvement, though it let the trade continue for twenty years.

author: madison
title: Other Powers
summary: Madison covers a range of other powers: copyrights and patents, a national capital, punishing treason, admitting new states, guaranteeing every state a republican government, paying old debts, amending the Constitution, and adopting it with approval from nine states.

author: madison
title: Limits on the States and the Supremacy of the Constitution
summary: Madison explains the limits placed on the states: no printing their own money, no laws that punish acts after the fact, and no laws breaking contracts. He defends the 'necessary and proper' clause and the rule that the Constitution and national laws are supreme over state laws.

author: madison
title: The States Are Not in Danger
summary: Madison argues that the national government's powers are 'few and defined,' while the states' powers are 'numerous and indefinite.' The national government will deal mostly with war, peace, and trade. The states will handle the daily concerns of people's lives. The point of government is the good of the people, not the power of either level of government.

author: madison
title: Comparing State and National Power
summary: Madison reminds readers that both the state and national governments are agents of the same people. People will naturally feel closer to their states. If the national government ever tried to grab too much power, the states and the armed citizens would resist together, and no national army could overcome them.

author: madison
title: What Separation of Powers Really Means
summary: Madison agrees that putting all power in the same hands is 'the very definition of tyranny.' But he shows that separation of powers, as explained by Montesquieu and practiced in Britain and the states, never meant the branches have nothing to do with each other. It means no branch should hold the whole power of another.

author: madison
title: Paper Rules Are Not Enough
summary: Madison argues that simply writing down boundaries between the branches won't stop them from overstepping. The legislature is the most dangerous branch in a republic because it is drawing all power into its 'impetuous vortex.' He gives examples from Virginia and Pennsylvania.

author: madison
title: Why Not Just Ask the People?
summary: Thomas Jefferson had suggested that when branches clash, a special convention of the people could settle it. Madison respects the idea but warns that frequent appeals would weaken respect for the government and stir up passions. Public reason, not public passion, should control the government.

author: madison
title: Scheduled Appeals to the People
summary: What about reviewing the government at regular intervals instead? Madison looks at Pennsylvania's Council of Censors, which did exactly that, and finds it was driven by party politics and failed to correct violations.

author: madison
title: Ambition Must Counteract Ambition
summary: One of the most important essays. Madison explains that the structure of the government itself must keep each branch in its place. Each branch gets the tools and motives to resist the others: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.' Because people are not angels, government needs both control by the people and built-in checks. Dividing power between national and state governments adds a 'double security' for rights.

author: madison
title: The House: Voters, Members, and Two-Year Terms
summary: Madison describes who can vote for and serve in the House of Representatives, and defends two-year terms. Frequent elections keep representatives dependent on the people, and two years is short enough to be safe.

author: madison
title: Why Two Years Instead of One?
summary: Madison answers the saying 'where annual elections end, tyranny begins.' National lawmakers need time to learn about a large and varied country, its laws, and foreign affairs. Two-year terms balance that need against keeping members accountable.

author: madison
title: The Three-Fifths Clause
summary: Madison explains how seats in the House are divided among the states by population, including the compromise that counted enslaved people as three-fifths of a person. He presents the argument as one a Southerner might make, treating enslaved people as both persons and property. The essay shows how the Constitution compromised with slavery.

author: madison
title: Is the House Too Small?
summary: Critics feared a House of only 65 members would be too small to represent the people. Madison argues that a group can be too large as well as too small. Big assemblies turn into mobs. He adds that while people need checks, they also have enough virtue to make self-government possible.

author: madison
title: Will the House Know Enough?
summary: Madison argues that a fairly small House can still understand the country's local interests, because national lawmakers need only general knowledge of the matters under national control, such as trade and taxes.

author: madison
title: Will the House Favor the Rich Few?
summary: Madison denies that the House will favor a wealthy elite. The voters are the great body of the people, rich and poor alike, and any citizen may serve. Representatives are tied to the people by frequent elections, gratitude, ambition, and the fact that they must live under the laws they make.

author: madison
title: The House Will Grow, and It Controls Money
summary: Madison explains that the House will grow as the census counts more people. He also stresses that the House controls money bills, and that the 'power over the purse' is the strongest tool the people's representatives have.

author: hamilton
title: Who Controls Federal Elections?
summary: Hamilton defends giving Congress the final say over the rules for federal elections. Every government should be able to protect its own existence. If states controlled federal elections completely, they could destroy the national government by refusing to hold them.

author: hamilton
title: Election Rules Won't Favor the Rich
summary: Hamilton dismisses the fear that Congress will rig election rules to favor the wealthy. The country is too diverse, the states are too watchful, and Congress has no power over who may vote.

author: hamilton
title: Where and When Elections Happen
summary: Hamilton answers the complaint that the Constitution doesn't require elections to be held locally. He adds that a uniform national election time is useful, because it prevents one faction from controlling the whole House at once.

author: madison
title: Why We Have a Senate
summary: Madison explains the Senate's design: older members, state legislatures choosing senators, equal votes for each state, and six-year terms. A second chamber guards against hasty or corrupt laws. He warns that laws that change constantly, or that are too long to read, hurt ordinary people and help the well-connected.

author: madison
title: The Senate as a Steadying Force
summary: Madison argues that a stable Senate will protect the nation's reputation abroad and protect the people from their own passing mistakes. When people are misled or swept up by passion, the Senate can slow things down until 'reason, justice, and truth' win out. He denies it will become an aristocracy.

author: jay
title: Making Treaties
summary: Jay explains why the president makes treaties with the approval of two-thirds of the Senate. Senators will be experienced and well-informed, and the president can act with the secrecy and speed diplomacy sometimes requires. Once made, treaties are law.

author: hamilton
title: Impeachment
summary: Hamilton explains why the Senate tries impeachments. Impeachable offenses come from the abuse of public trust and are political in nature, so the trial will stir strong party feelings. The Senate is independent and numerous enough to judge fairly. A conviction only removes someone from office; criminal trials can follow in regular courts.

author: hamilton
title: Answering Objections to Impeachment Trials
summary: Hamilton answers objections that letting the Senate try impeachments mixes up the branches or gives the Senate too much power. He notes the House alone can bring charges, and senators will have no reason to protect officials who abuse power.

author: hamilton
title: Scare Tactics About the Presidency
summary: Hamilton says opponents have painted the presidency as a monarchy in disguise. He exposes one false claim, that the president can fill Senate vacancies, as an example of how the office has been misrepresented.

author: hamilton
title: The Electoral College
summary: Hamilton defends how the president is chosen. Electors chosen in each state meet separately, which he believes reflects the people's wishes while preventing plots, bribery, and foreign influence. He predicts the system will make it unlikely that anyone lacking real ability will win the office.

author: hamilton
title: A President Is Not a King
summary: Hamilton compares the president to the British king and the governor of New York. The president is elected for four years, can be impeached and removed, has a veto that can be overridden, cannot declare war, and needs the Senate for treaties and appointments. The king has none of these limits.

author: hamilton
title: Energy in the Executive
summary: Hamilton argues that good government needs an energetic executive, able to act quickly and firmly. That requires a single president, not a committee. When power is shared among several people, it is harder to act and easier to hide who is responsible for mistakes. One person can be held accountable.

author: hamilton
title: Why a Four-Year Term
summary: Hamilton argues that the president needs a long enough term to act with independence. Serving the people does not mean obeying every sudden shift in public mood. Sometimes leaders must resist a passing passion until people have time to think it over.

author: hamilton
title: Should Presidents Be Re-Elected?
summary: Hamilton opposes term limits for the president. The chance at re-election encourages good behavior, keeps experienced leaders available in emergencies, and lets voters keep a president they trust. Forcing presidents out might push ambitious ones to grab power instead.

author: hamilton
title: The President's Salary and the Veto
summary: Hamilton explains that Congress can't raise or cut the president's pay during a term, so it can't bribe or starve the president. The veto lets the president defend the office against Congress and block bad laws, while Congress can still override with a two-thirds vote.

author: hamilton
title: Commander in Chief and the Pardon Power
summary: Hamilton explains why the president commands the military: directing war requires the leadership of one person. He also defends the pardon power. One person will feel the weight of responsibility for mercy, and a timely pardon can help end a rebellion.

author: hamilton
title: Sharing the Treaty Power
summary: Hamilton explains why treaties need both the president and two-thirds of the Senate. Treaties are like laws and also like deals with foreign nations, so they shouldn't belong to the president alone. The House is too large and changes too often to handle them.

author: hamilton
title: Appointing Officials
summary: Hamilton defends the president's power to nominate officials with the Senate's approval. One person will choose more carefully and feel more responsible than a group. The Senate's role guards against favoritism and unfit choices.

author: hamilton
title: The President's Other Powers
summary: Hamilton finishes his discussion of the presidency, covering the State of the Union, receiving ambassadors, and calling Congress into session. He concludes that the presidency combines the energy good government needs with the safety a republic requires.

author: hamilton
title: The Courts and Judicial Review
summary: Hamilton calls the courts the 'least dangerous' branch, since they have 'neither force nor will, but merely judgment.' Judges serve during good behavior so they can be independent. When a law conflicts with the Constitution, judges must follow the Constitution, because it expresses the will of the people. This idea became known as judicial review.

author: hamilton
title: Judges' Pay and Accountability
summary: Hamilton explains that Congress cannot lower judges' salaries while they serve, because power over a person's paycheck is power over their will. Judges can still be impeached for misconduct.

author: hamilton
title: What Cases Federal Courts Hear
summary: Hamilton explains which cases belong in federal courts: those involving the Constitution and national laws, treaties, ambassadors, cases at sea, and disputes between states or between citizens of different states. These cases affect the whole nation or need a neutral judge.

author: hamilton
title: The Supreme Court and Its Jurisdiction
summary: Hamilton defends a separate Supreme Court rather than letting a branch of the legislature serve as the highest court, as Britain did. He explains the difference between cases the Supreme Court hears first and cases it hears on appeal, and argues states can't be sued by individuals without their consent.

author: hamilton
title: State Courts and Federal Courts
summary: Hamilton explains that state courts will keep their power to hear many cases, even those involving national law, and that appeals from them can go to the Supreme Court. The two court systems will work as parts of one whole.

author: hamilton
title: Trial by Jury
summary: The longest essay. Hamilton answers the charge that the Constitution abolishes jury trials in civil (non-criminal) cases. Silence about something is not a ban. State practices differ so much that a single national rule would have been hard to write, and Congress can provide for juries where needed.

author: hamilton
title: Is a Bill of Rights Necessary?
summary: Hamilton argues that a bill of rights is unnecessary and could even be dangerous. The Constitution already protects key rights, like habeas corpus and jury trials in criminal cases. Listing exceptions to powers never granted might suggest those powers exist. In a real sense, he says, the Constitution itself is a bill of rights. The country added one anyway in 1791.

author: hamilton
title: Closing Arguments
summary: Hamilton wraps up. He admits the Constitution isn't perfect but argues it should be adopted now and improved later through amendments, which will be easier than renegotiating the whole plan. A nation without a national government, he says, is 'an awful spectacle.'
